from math import sqrt, sin, cos
from itertools import combinations
s=1/sqrt(2)
X=[[1.,0.],[0.,s],[0.,s]]
C=[[0.,0.],[1.5,0.],[-1.5,0.]]
def F(Y): return sum(C[i][j]*Y[i][j]+abs(Y[i][j]) for i in range(3) for j in range(2))
def rotate(pair,t):
 Y=[r[:] for r in X]; i,j=pair
 for c in range(2):
  Y[i][c]=cos(t)*X[i][c]+sin(t)*X[j][c]
  Y[j][c]=-sin(t)*X[i][c]+cos(t)*X[j][c]
 return Y
step=1e-7
print('Theorem 5.5(c) check: F=f+||X||1, f=1.5*(X21-X31), X=',X)
for pair in combinations(range(3),2):
 print('Pair',tuple(i+1 for i in pair),'left derivative',(F(rotate(pair,-step))-F(X))/(-step),'right derivative',(F(rotate(pair,step))-F(X))/step)
print('Common KKT subgradient requires s12 >=',.5/s,'and s12 <=',-.5/s)
for t in [1e-3,1e-5,1e-7]:
 # Exact feasible curve: rotate the first column toward (0,-1,1)/sqrt(2); keep second column fixed.
 Y=[[cos(sqrt(2)*t),0.],[-sin(sqrt(2)*t)/sqrt(2),s],[sin(sqrt(2)*t)/sqrt(2),s]]
 gram=[[sum(Y[i][a]*Y[i][b] for i in range(3)) for b in range(2)] for a in range(2)]
 print('t',t,'feasible Gram',gram,'full-direction objective derivative',(F(Y)-F(X))/t)
print('Lemma 6.6(b) smooth check: n=r=3, k=2, X=I3, f=<G,X>, G12=1, G21=-1')
full=2*sqrt(2); expected_block=full/3; gamma=sqrt(3)
print('full residual',full,'claimed upper bound',gamma*expected_block)

from math import sin,cos,sqrt,pi
s=1/sqrt(2)
X=[[1.,0.],[0.,s],[0.,s]]
C=[[0.,0.],[1.5,0.],[-1.5,0.]]
def F(Y): return sum(C[i][j]*Y[i][j]+abs(Y[i][j]) for i in range(3) for j in range(2))
f0=F(X)
for pair in [(0,1),(0,2),(1,2)]:
 for kind in ['rotation','reflection']:
  best=(float('inf'),None)
  for z in range(20001):
   angle=2*pi*z/20000; c=cos(angle); t=sin(angle)
   V=[[c,t],[-t,c]] if kind=='rotation' else [[-c,t],[t,c]]

   prox=.5*sum((V[a][b]-(1 if a==b else 0))**2 for a in range(2) for b in range(2))
   val=F(Y)-f0+prox
   if val<best[0]:best=(val,angle)

strengths: The row-wise orthogonal update preserves the Gram matrix exactly and accommodates rectangular Stiefel constraints. The feasibility and sufficient-decrease arguments are useful foundations.
Reducing two-row updates to rotations and reflections yields practical low-dimensional subproblems. The sampled working-set strategies are also reasonable computational ideas.

Experiments cover four objective classes, ten datasets, multiple ranks and regularization strengths, and relevant baselines including ManPG and OptM. Many reported objective improvements are substantial.
weaknesses: The central stationarity equivalence in Theorem 5.5(c) is false under the stated assumptions. Consider X=[[1,0],[0,1/√2],[0,1/√2]], h(X)=||X||₁, and f(X)=1.5(X₂₁−X₃₁). Every two-row subproblem is stationary at V=I₂, yet the feasible tangent direction [[0,0],[-1,0],[1,0]] has objective directional derivative −1. With Q=0 and θ=1, X even minimizes every exact block subproblem. Appendix B.8 incorrectly infers the existence of one common subgradient from separate, potentially incompatible subgradients for individual blocks. This undermines the claimed stronger-than-critical optimality guarantee.

The strong-convergence analysis contains additional substantive errors. Lemma 6.6(b) fails even for n=r=3, k=2, X=I₃ and f(X)=X₁₂−X₂₁: its full residual is 2√2, while the asserted upper bound is 2√(2/3). The proof confuses a root-mean-square bound with a mean bound. Appendix B.10 also exchanges the previous and next sampled blocks inside an expectation despite the updated iterate depending on the previous block. Consequently, Theorem 6.8 is not established by the supplied argument.

The claimed globally exact breakpoint solver is incorrect as specified. Section 7.1 omits the cos(θ)=0 cases from the tangent parameterization, lists xᵢ/yᵢ rather than −xᵢ/yᵢ as zeros of x+ty, and incorrectly discards yᵢ=0 terms: for the ℓ1 penalty, these still contribute |xᵢ|/√(1+t²). These issues directly affect the exact-subproblem assumption used by the algorithm and theory.

The guarantees do not substantiate the advertised breadth. Uniformly bounded subgradients in Assumption 6.1 are unavailable for ℓ0 penalties at zero and indicator normal cones at boundaries. The expectation proofs assume uniform random block selection, leaving the practical greedy variants insufficiently covered. Section 7.2 also omits the proximal term from Equation (11) when describing FIM, without establishing the required sufficient decrease.

The empirical comparisons need stronger controls. Only OBCD's breakpoint routine receives a C++ implementation, complicating attribution of wall-clock gains. Warm-start experiments give OBCD an additional ten seconds without corresponding baseline-continuation controls. No repeated-run uncertainty, matched stationarity targets, or convincing scaling study establishes robust efficiency or stronger terminal stationarity.

Reproducibility contains a concrete feasibility inconsistency: Section 9.1 initializes nonnegative columns using 1/|Gᵢ|, giving squared column norm 1/|Gᵢ| instead of 1. Since OBCD preserves the Gram matrix, this cannot produce the reported near-machine-precision orthogonality without an unreported correction. Data preprocessing, sampled subsets, seeds, baseline tuning, and the complete implementation location are also insufficiently specified.
